text: Two short sessions on different days beat one long session. Memory consolidates between them.
Forgetting a little before you review is a feature. Relearning after a gap makes the memory stick harder.
If the exam is a month away, spread reviews about a week apart. The best gap grows with the deadline.
Cramming works for tomorrow and fails for next month. Spaced practice reverses that.
Closing the book and recalling what you read strengthens memory more than reading it again.
Self-testing feels worse than rereading while you do it, and produces better exam scores. Trust the result, not the feeling.
Rereading and highlighting rank near the bottom of study techniques. Practice testing ranks near the top.
Write down everything you remember from a chapter before checking. The gaps you find are your study plan.
Getting a practice question wrong and then seeing the answer teaches more than reading the answer first.
Flashcards work because of the effort to recall, not the card. Do not flip too early.
Mixing problem types in one session feels harder but improves your ability to pick the right method later.
Blocked practice inflates confidence during study and drops off on the test. Interleave to keep both honest.
Alternate between two subjects in an evening rather than finishing one before starting the next.
Sleep after studying is part of studying. Consolidation happens overnight.
An all-nighter costs more memory than it buys. Sleep-deprived brains encode new material poorly.
Reviewing shortly before sleep, then again in the morning, uses the night as a free study session.
A short nap after learning protects the new memory from being overwritten by the rest of the day.
People reliably underestimate how long tasks take. Add a margin to your estimate.
Estimate by looking at how long similar tasks actually took you, not by imagining this one going smoothly.
Breaking a task into parts and estimating each part reduces the underestimate, but rarely removes it.
Deciding when and where you will study roughly doubles the odds that you actually do.
Phrase the plan as a trigger: after lunch, at the library, open the problem set. Vague intentions fade.
Plan for the obstacle too: if my phone is nearby, it goes in the bag. Naming the if makes the then automatic.
New habits take weeks to months to feel automatic. Missing a single day barely dents the curve.
Attach studying to something you already do daily. The existing routine becomes the reminder.
Switching tasks costs time on every switch, even for people who feel good at it.
A phone on the desk drains attention even face down and silent. Out of sight is the cheapest focus tool.
Short breaks restore attention on long tasks. Working through them makes the later minutes worth less.
Asking why a fact is true, and answering in your own words, builds memory better than repeating it.
Explaining a solution to yourself step by step catches misunderstandings that silent reading hides.
Fluency is not knowledge. Material that feels familiar after rereading is often not retrievable on the test.
Predict your score before a practice test, then compare. Calibrating your confidence is itself a study skill.
Treating a wrong answer as information rather than a verdict keeps you working on the hard problems longer.
Trying to produce an answer before you are shown it, even a guess, improves later recall of the right one.
A quick sketch next to your notes gives the idea a second route into memory.
